newsitem.title: USA: New York City to sue U.S. over welfare-immigration.
newsitem.headline: New York City to sue U.S. over welfare-immigration.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani said he will sue the federal government on Friday to challenge the constitutionality of U.S. immigration and welfare reforms targeting illegal aliens.

In a speech at Harvard University's John F. Kennedy School of Government on Thursday night, Giuliani said the immigration and welfare reforms recently passed by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton were "inherently unfair ... and totally inconsistent with why America has become as great a place as it is."
The reforms are aimed at clamping down on illegal immigration, and contain provisions designed to make it more difficult for illegal aliens to take advantage of basic social services.

Since 1988, however, New York City has given illegal or undocumented immigrants access to critical services such as schools, police and hospitals and mandated that their names not be revealed to federal authorities, Giuliani said.

"I know that our executive order has angered some people in Washington and this year, they passed laws that would overturn it," he said, referring to Section 434 of the new welfare reform measure and Section 642 of the immigration law, which severely restrict any immigrant's access to services.
He defended the New York executive order saying it not only protects aliens, particularly illegal aliens, but "it protects the rest of society as well."

New York City, which has between 400,000 and 450,000 illegal aliens, would be facing between 70,000 and 80,000 children "out on the streets, out of school ... it makes the city less safe," said the mayor.
"Muggers don't like to check for green cards," he said, adding that the police department "relies to a significant degree on the information from people who are illegal or undocumented aliens."

Giuliani, the grandson of an immigrant, said he would base his legal challenge on the 10th Amendment, which gives states the right to determine policies not expressly granted to the federal government by the Constitution.
"The only thing I really know how to do is sue," the former U.S. Attorney jokingly told the crowd.
